quotes.t: Mathematics would certainly not have come into existence if one had known from the beginning that there was in nature no exactly straight line, no actual circle, no absolute magnitude.
He who thinks a great deal is not suited to be a party man: he thinks his way through the party and out the other side too soon.
I teach you the overman. Man is something that shall be overcome. What have you done to overcome him?
I have fought against white domination, and I have fought against black domination.
quotes.source: "I Am Prepared to Die" (Rivonia Trial statement, 20 April 1964)

quotes.t: I was not a messiah, but an ordinary man who had become a leader because of extraordinary circumstances.
When a man is denied the right to live the life he believes in, he has no choice but to become an outlaw.
If the soul is left in darkness, sins will be committed. The guilty one is not he who commits the sin, but the one who causes the darkness.
So long as ignorance and misery remain on earth, books like this cannot be useless.
The delight we inspire in others has this enchanting peculiarity that, far from being diminished like every other reflection, it returns to us more radiant than ever.
Only it takes time to be happy. A lot of time. Happiness, too, is a long patience.
It takes time to live. Like any work of art, life needs to be thought about.
But in the end one needs more courage to live than to kill himself.
Part of me suspects that I'm a loser, and the other part of me thinks I'm God Almighty.
It's better to fade away like an old soldier than to burn out.
I don't stand back and judge — I do.
The power of accurate observation is commonly called cynicism by those who have not got it.
A government that robs Peter to pay Paul can always depend on the support of Paul.
A lifetime of happiness! No man alive could bear it: it would be hell on earth.
Not to be born is, past all prizing, best.
Reason is God's crowning gift to man.
In a just cause the weak o'ercome the strong.
To the question whether I am a pessimist or an optimist, I answer that my knowledge is pessimistic, but my willing and hoping are optimistic.
quotes.source: Out of My Life and Thought (1933)

quotes.t: Modern man no longer knows how to foresee or to forestall. He will end by destroying the earth.
If a man loses his reverence for any part of life, he will lose his reverence for all of life.
Great ambition is the passion of a great character.
Ambition never is in a greater hurry than I; it merely keeps pace with circumstances and with my general way of thinking.

Many a one commits a reprehensible action, who is at bottom an honourable man, because man seldom acts upon natural impulse, but from some secret passion of the moment which lies hidden and concealed within the narrowest folds of his heart.
The only reason we don't open our hearts and minds to other people is that they trigger confusion in us that we don't feel brave enough or sane enough to deal with.
When we hold on to our opinions with aggression, no matter how valid our cause, we are simply adding more aggression to the planet, and violence and pain increase.
It's a transformative experience to simply pause instead of immediately filling up the space.
If you are planning for a year, sow rice; if you are planning for a decade, plant trees; if you are planning for a lifetime, educate people.
A man without a smiling face should not open a shop.
An inch of gold will not buy an inch of time.
But do not ask me where I am going, as I travel in this limitless world, where every step I take is my home.
quotes.source: The Zen Poetry of Dōgen (trans. Steven Heine, 1997)

quotes.t: Yet you must not cling to the words of the old sages either; they, too, may not be right. Even if you believe them, you should be alert so that, in the event that something superior comes along, you may follow that.
If he cannot stop the mind that seeks after fame and profit, he will spend his life without finding peace.
There are a thousand hacking at the branches of evil to one who is striking at the root.
The law will never make men free; it is men who have got to make the law free.
It is a great art to saunter.
We must constantly remind ourselves that whatever our religion or creed, we are all one people.
quotes.source: Radio address to the Defence Services (1 December 1947)

quotes.t: Peace is not only an absolute necessity for us in India in order to progress and develop but also of paramount importance to the world.
Great causes and little men go ill together.
Let every man remind their descendants that they also are soldiers who must not desert the ranks of their ancestors, or from cowardice fall behind.
Friends have all things in common.
Rhetoric, it seems, is a producer of persuasion for belief, not for instruction in the matter of right and wrong.
I am not an Athenian or a Greek, but a citizen of the world.
Having the fewest wants, I am nearest to the gods.
quotes.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers

quotes.t: Crito, I owe a cock to Asclepius; will you remember to pay the debt?
Man is free at the instant he wants to be.
What we find in books is like the fire in our hearths. We fetch it from our neighbors, we kindle it at home, we communicate it to others, and it becomes the property of all.
Where there is friendship, there is our natural soil.
Take nothing on its looks; take everything on evidence. There's no better rule.
To conceal anything from those to whom I am attached, is not in my nature. I can never close my lips where I have opened my heart.
Pip, dear old chap, life is made of ever so many partings welded together, as I may say.
My friends are my "estate." Forgive me then the avarice to hoard them.
We turn not older with years, but newer every day.
Success is counted sweetest by those who ne'er succeed.
Remember that time is money.
He that would live in peace and at ease, must not speak all he knows, nor judge all he sees.
Human felicity is produced not so much by great pieces of good fortune that seldom happen, as by little advantages that occur every day.
I have consistently preached that nonviolence demands that the means we use must be as pure as the ends we seek.
She had been forced into prudence in her youth, she learned romance as she grew older: the natural sequel of an unnatural beginning.
The hero of my tale, whom I love with all the power of my soul, whom I have tried to portray in all his beauty, who has been, is, and will be beautiful, is Truth.
The writer's responsibility is to increase, develop our senses, expand our vision, heighten our awareness and enrich our articulateness.
quotes.source: The Diary of Anaïs Nin, Vol. 5

quotes.t: I have often been downcast, but never in despair.
quotes.source: The Diary of a Young Girl (1942–1944)

quotes.t: Love in action is a harsh and dreadful thing compared with love in dreams.
Forgiveness says you are given another chance to make a new beginning.
Audacity augments courage; hesitation, fear.
Silence is the element in which great things fashion themselves together; that at length they may emerge, full-formed and majestic, into the daylight of Life, which they are thenceforth to rule.
Yet it is in our idleness, in our dreams, that the submerged truth sometimes comes to the top.
quotes.source: A Room of One's Own (1929), Ch. 2

quotes.t: The companions of our childhood always possess a certain power over our minds which hardly any later friend can obtain.
What the imagination seizes as Beauty must be truth — whether it existed before or not.
Caste is a notion; it is a state of the mind.
It is truth that liberates, not your effort to be free.
If you want work well done, select a busy man; the other kind has no time.
quotes.source: The Note Book of Elbert Hubbard (1927)

quotes.t: I never considered a difference of opinion in politics, in religion, in philosophy, as cause for withdrawing from a friend.
Sometimes life hits you in the head with a brick. Don't lose faith.
It is of immense importance to learn to laugh at ourselves.
quotes.source: The Journal of Katherine Mansfield, journal entry, October 1922

quotes.t: We are ever striving for what is forbidden, and are desiring what is denied us.
quotes.source: Amores, Book 3, Elegy 4 (tr. Henry T. Riley)

quotes.t: It is in vain to say human beings ought to be satisfied with tranquillity: they must have action; and they will make it if they cannot find it.
For it is not light that is needed, but fire; it is not the gentle shower, but thunder. We need the storm, the whirlwind, and the earthquake.
quotes.source: What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July? (5 July 1852)

quotes.t: Happiness, not in another place but this place, not for another hour but this hour.
quotes.source: Give Me the Splendid Silent Sun, Leaves of Grass

quotes.t: The shifts of fortune test the reliability of friends.
All things are possible until they are proved impossible — and even the impossible may only be so, as of now.
The primary cause of unhappiness is never the situation but your thoughts about it.
The reading of all good books is like conversation with the finest men of past centuries.
quotes.source: Discourse on the Method, Part I (1637)

quotes.t: Religion is the sigh of the oppressed creature, the heart of a heartless world, and the soul of soulless conditions.
quotes.source: A Contribution to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right, Introduction (1844)

quotes.t: Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent.
For the great doesn't happen through impulse alone, and is a succession of little things that are brought together.
quotes.source: Letter to Theo van Gogh, 22 October 1882 (Letter 274)

quotes.t: The moment you doubt whether you can fly, you cease for ever to be able to do it.
quotes.source: Peter Pan in Kensington Gardens, Ch. II (1906)

quotes.t: Logic may indeed be unshakeable, but it cannot withstand a man who is determined to live.
The heaviest of burdens crushes us, we sink beneath it, it pins us to the ground.
quotes.source: The Unbearable Lightness of Being, Part 1 (1984)

quotes.t: More than ever before in human history, we share a common destiny. We can master it only if we face it together. And that, my friends, is why we have the United Nations.
quotes.source: Nobel Peace Prize lecture, Oslo, 10 December 2001

quotes.t: We were the people who were not in the papers. We lived in the blank white spaces at the edges of print. It gave us more freedom.
The sole substitute for an experience which we have not ourselves lived through is art and literature.
Man's main task in life is to give birth to himself, to become what he potentially is.
Man is nostalgia and a search for communion.
quotes.source: The Labyrinth of Solitude, Ch. 9 (1950; Lysander Kemp translation, 1961)

quotes.t: In summer the nights. Not only when the moon shines, but on dark nights too, as the fireflies flit to and fro, and even when it rains, how beautiful it is!
quotes.source: The Pillow Book, §1, tr. Ivan Morris (1967)

quotes.t: The Orient was almost a European invention, and had been since antiquity a place of romance, exotic beings, haunting memories and landscapes, remarkable experiences.
There is no death, daughter. People die only when we forget them.

Albert Camus.bio: French-Algerian writer and philosopher, author of The Stranger; Nobel Prize in Literature 1957.

Albert Schweitzer.bio: Albert Schweitzer was an Alsatian theologian, musician and physician who founded a hospital at Lambaréné in Gabon and served there for decades. His philosophy of reverence for life and his Bach scholarship earned him the Nobel Peace Prize in 1952.

Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn.bio: Russian writer and dissident, author of The Gulag Archipelago; Nobel Prize in Literature 1970.

Anais Nin.bio: Anaïs Nin, French-born American diarist and novelist. She is celebrated for her multi-volume Diary, begun when she was eleven, and for works such as Delta of Venus.

Anne Frank.bio: German-born Jewish diarist whose diary documents life in hiding during the Holocaust.

B.R. Ambedkar.bio: Indian jurist and social reformer who chaired the drafting of India's Constitution and campaigned against caste discrimination.

Benjamin Franklin.bio: American polymath - printer, scientist, diplomat - and a Founding Father of the United States.

Charles Dickens.bio: English novelist and social critic; author of A Christmas Carol, Oliver Twist and Great Expectations.

Charlotte Brontë.bio: English novelist, author of Jane Eyre.
Charlotte Brontë.credit: Alonzo Chappel, Public domain (File: File:Charlotte Bronte by Alonzo Chappel.jpg)

Cicero.bio: Marcus Tullius Cicero was a Roman statesman, lawyer and orator considered the master of Latin prose. His speeches, letters and philosophical works, including On Friendship, transmitted Greek philosophy to the Roman world.

Desmond Tutu.bio: South African Anglican archbishop and Nobel Peace Prize laureate (1984) who campaigned against apartheid.

Dogen.bio: Founder of the Sōtō school of Zen in Japan and author of the Shōbōgenzō, a landmark of Buddhist philosophy.

Eckhart Tolle.bio: Eckhart Tolle is a German-born spiritual teacher living in Canada, author of The Power of Now (1997) and A New Earth (2005), books on presence and the ego that became international bestsellers.

Edward Said.bio: Palestinian-American scholar who founded postcolonial studies with Orientalism (1978).

Elbert Hubbard.bio: Elbert Hubbard was an American writer, publisher and philosopher who founded the Roycroft arts-and-crafts community. His essay "A Message to Garcia" (1899) was one of the most widely reprinted works of its era; he died in the sinking of the Lusitania.

Emily Dickinson.bio: American poet whose nearly 1,800 poems, mostly unpublished in her lifetime, made her a central figure of American literature.
Emily Dickinson.credit: Miscellaneous Items in High Demand, PPOC, Library of Congress, Public domain

Erich Fromm.bio: German social psychologist and humanistic philosopher, author of The Art of Loving.

Franz Kafka.bio: Czech writer, author of The Trial and The Metamorphosis.

Frederick Douglass.bio: American abolitionist and writer who escaped slavery and became a leading voice against it.

Friedrich Nietzsche.bio: German philosopher known for Thus Spoke Zarathustra and the concept of the will to power.

Fyodor Dostoevsky.bio: Russian novelist, author of Crime and Punishment and The Brothers Karamazov.

George Bernard Shaw.bio: Irish playwright and critic; author of Pygmalion; Nobel Prize in Literature 1925.
George Bernard Shaw.credit: Sussman, Public domain (File: George Bernard Shaw, playwright (SAYRE 9001).jpg)

Henry David Thoreau.bio: American writer known for Walden (1854) and the essay Civil Disobedience.

Isabel Allende.bio: Chilean-American novelist whose debut The House of the Spirits (1982) became a landmark of magical realism. One of the most widely read Spanish-language authors in the world, she writes sweeping family sagas of love, exile and memory.

J.M. Barrie.bio: Scottish novelist and playwright, creator of Peter Pan.

Jane Austen.bio: English novelist known for Pride and Prejudice and Emma, celebrated for irony and social observation.
Jane Austen.credit: Engraving by William Home Lizars after James Andrews, Public domain

Jawaharlal Nehru.bio: Leader of India's independence movement and the country's first Prime Minister (1947-1964).

Jiddu Krishnamurti.bio: Indian philosopher and speaker on the nature of mind, meditation, and human freedom; rejected all guru roles.

John Keats.bio: English Romantic poet of the great Odes, including Ode to a Nightingale.

John Lennon.bio: English singer-songwriter, co-founder of the Beatles and solo artist known for Imagine.

Karl Marx.bio: German philosopher and economist, co-author of The Communist Manifesto.
Karl Marx.credit: John Jabez Edwin Mayall, Public domain

Katherine Mansfield.bio: New Zealand modernist short-story writer, a leading figure of early 20th-century literature alongside Joyce and Woolf.
Katherine Mansfield.credit: Archives New Zealand from New Zealand, CC BY-SA 2.0

Kofi Annan.bio: Ghanaian diplomat who served as UN Secretary-General from 1997 to 2006 and won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2001.

Leo Tolstoy.bio: Russian novelist, author of War and Peace and Anna Karenina.

Ludwig Wittgenstein.bio: Austrian philosopher whose Tractatus and Philosophical Investigations reshaped 20th-century philosophy.

Margaret Atwood.bio: Margaret Atwood is a Canadian novelist, poet and essayist best known for The Handmaid's Tale, her dystopian novel that became a global cultural phenomenon. She has twice won the Booker Prize, for The Blind Assassin and The Testaments.

Martin Luther King Jr..bio: American Baptist minister who led the civil rights movement; Nobel Peace Prize laureate 1964.

Mary Shelley.bio: English novelist, author of Frankenstein, a founding work of science fiction.

Milan Kundera.bio: Czech-French novelist, author of The Unbearable Lightness of Being.

Napoleon Bonaparte.bio: Napoleon Bonaparte was a French military leader who rose to prominence during the French Revolution and became Emperor of the French in 1804. His Napoleonic Wars reshaped Europe, and his Napoleonic Code influenced legal systems worldwide. He died in exile on Saint Helena.

Nelson Mandela.role: Anti-apartheid leader, President of South Africa
Nelson Mandela.bio: South African anti-apartheid revolutionary who spent 27 years in prison and became the country's first Black president in 1994.

Octavio Paz.bio: Mexican poet, essayist and diplomat, winner of the Nobel Prize in Literature (1990). His essay The Labyrinth of Solitude is a landmark meditation on Mexican identity, and his poetry bridges Mexican and European modernism.

Ovid.bio: Ovid was a Roman poet celebrated for the Metamorphoses, a vast narrative poem of mythological transformations. Exiled by the emperor Augustus to the Black Sea coast, he spent his last decade writing poems of lament and endurance.

Pearl Buck.bio: Pearl S. Buck was an American writer who spent much of her early life in China, where her parents were missionaries. Her novel The Good Earth won the Pulitzer Prize, and she received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1938.

Pema Chodron.bio: Pema Chodron is an American nun in the Tibetan Buddhist tradition and a widely read author and teacher. Her books, including When Things Fall Apart, bring Buddhist teachings on compassion and difficulty to a broad audience.

Plato.bio: Greek philosopher, student of Socrates and author of The Republic.

Publilius Syrus.bio: Publilius Syrus was a Latin writer of the 1st century BC who was brought to Italy as a slave from Syria and later freed. He is known for his Sententiae, a collection of moral maxims drawn from his mimes.

René Descartes.bio: French philosopher and mathematician, founder of modern rationalism.

Sei Shōnagon.bio: Heian-era court lady (c. 966–c. 1017) whose Pillow Book, a collection of observations and lists, is a masterpiece of Japanese literature.

Socrates.bio: Greek philosopher of Athens, central figure of Western philosophy; left no writings.

Sophocles.bio: Sophocles was an Athenian tragedian who wrote more than 120 plays, of which seven survive complete. Oedipus Rex and Antigone, his most famous works, set the pattern for Western tragedy.

Steve Jobs.bio: Co-founder of Apple, Steve Jobs helped launch the personal computer era and later reinvented music, phones and tablets with the iPod, iPhone and iPad. Forced out of Apple in 1985, he founded NeXT and built Pixar into a major studio before returning in 1997 to rescue the company he had started.

Thomas Carlyle.bio: Thomas Carlyle was a Scottish historian, philosopher and essayist whose works, including Sartor Resartus and On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History, shaped Victorian thought. His history of the French Revolution is regarded as a classic of the genre.

Thomas Jefferson.bio: Thomas Jefferson was an American statesman and Founding Father who wrote the Declaration of Independence and served as the third President of the United States (1801–1809). He founded the University of Virginia and doubled the nation's size with the Louisiana Purchase.

Victor Hugo.bio: French poet and novelist, author of Les Misérables and The Hunchback of Notre-Dame.
Victor Hugo.credit: Étienne Carjat, Public domain (File: Victor Hugo by Étienne Carjat 1876 - full.jpg)

Vincent van Gogh.bio: Dutch Post-Impressionist painter of The Starry Night and Sunflowers.

Virginia Woolf.bio: Virginia Woolf was an English writer and a central figure of literary modernism, famous for stream-of-consciousness novels such as Mrs Dalloway (1925) and To the Lighthouse (1927). Her essay A Room of One's Own (1929) became a foundational feminist text on women and writing. With her husband Leonard she founded the Hogarth Press, which published her own work and that of T. S. Eliot and others.

Voltaire.bio: Voltaire, born François-Marie Arouet, was a French Enlightenment writer, philosopher and historian famous for the novella Candide and for his witty defence of civil liberties, including freedom of speech and religion. He was one of the most prolific and influential writers of his age.

Walt Whitman.bio: American poet best known for the collection Leaves of Grass (1855).
